quick: Heart failure edema: 10-20 mg once daily; hypertension: 5 mg once daily
Use only if clearly needed; diuretics generally avoided
Limited data; caution - may affect milk/monitor infant
Initial 20 mg once daily in chronic renal failure; titrate
Cirrhosis: start 5-10 mg with aldosterone antagonist; max studied 40 mg
Electrolytes (K, Na, Mg), renal function, BP, fluid status
summary: Torasemide (torsemide) is a loop diuretic for edema from heart failure, renal disease, or hepatic disease, and for hypertension. It has higher and more predictable oral bioavailability and a longer duration than furosemide. Key cautions are electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia), dehydration, and ototoxicity at high doses.
indications: Edema associated with hepatic disease (e.g., cirrhosis)

dosage.d: Initial 10 or 20 mg once daily; titrate by doubling
Initial 20 mg once daily; titrate by doubling
Initial 5 or 10 mg once daily with an aldosterone antagonist or potassium-sparing diuretic
Initial 5 mg once daily; increase to 10 mg after 4-6 weeks if needed
dosage.n: Add another agent if 10 mg insufficient

admin: May be taken with or without food
Best taken in the morning to avoid nocturia
Oral and IV doses are interchangeable 1:1 (high oral bioavailability)
Titrate to clinical response and weight/fluid status
moa: Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, blocking reabsorption of sodium and chloride. This produces a potent diuresis with loss of water, sodium, potassium, and other electrolytes. Also has some aldosterone-antagonist-like and vasodilatory effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to torasemide or sulfonylureas
relative: Hepatic cirrhosis (risk of sudden fluid/electrolyte shifts)

preg: Use only if clearly needed. Diuretics are generally not used to treat gestational hypertension/edema because they can reduce placental perfusion. Limited human data.
lact: It is not known whether torasemide is excreted in human milk; related loop diuretics can suppress lactation. Use with caution and monitor the infant.
renal: Used in chronic renal failure with edema; initiate at 20 mg once daily and titrate. Higher doses may be required; doses above 200 mg/day have not been studied. Monitor electrolytes and renal function closely.
hepatic: In hepatic cirrhosis with edema/ascites, use cautiously with an aldosterone antagonist or potassium-sparing diuretic; start 5-10 mg once daily, doses above 40 mg not studied. Avoid in hepatic coma.

moderate: ACE inhibitors/ARBs (hypotension, renal effects on initiation)
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excess - additive hypotension and dehydration
interactions.diagnostics: Can raise uric acid, glucose, cholesterol; alters electrolytes

monitoring: Hearing in patients on high/IV doses
counsel: Take in the morning to limit night-time urination
Report muscle cramps, weakness, palpitations, or excessive thirst (electrolyte loss)
Maintain potassium intake as advised; do not start salt substitutes without advice
Weigh yourself regularly if you have heart failure
pk: Diuresis within ~1 hour of oral dose
pearls: Oral bioavailability ~80-90% and predictable - oral and IV doses are roughly equivalent (vs furosemide ~50%)
Longer duration and less ototoxicity than equivalent furosemide doses
Partly hepatically metabolized, so usable when renal function is poor
TRANSFORM-HF trial showed similar outcomes to furosemide in heart failure
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered if it is early in the day; if it is late or near bedtime, skip it to avoid night-time urination. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose causes excessive diuresis with dehydration, hypotension, electrolyte depletion, and possible circulatory collapse. Management is supportive: fluid and electrolyte replacement and monitoring. There is no specific antidote.
